newsitem.title: UK: Stalemate on American deal adds to BA woes.
newsitem.headline: Stalemate on American deal adds to BA woes.

text.p: Reports that British Airways Plc's proposed alliance with American Airlines remained locked in regulatory stalemate added to the British company's woes on Wednesday, helping to depress its share price.
Britain's Trade and Industry Secretary Margaret Beckett met with EU competition commissioner Karel van Miert on Tuesday to discuss the BA/AA alliance.
But efforts to try and break the impasse over terms for clearing the deal ended in failure, said a report in the Financial Times on Wednesday.
The report said the issue of the number of slots controlled by the transatlantic alliance at London's Heathrow airport -- the world's busiest -- remained the key sticking point.

Fears for the alliance's prospects weighed on BA's shares on Wednesday, with the impact of a likely BA cabin crew strike next week adding further pressure. Shares in BA were down 11 1/2 pence at 683 in late morning trading.
The British Department of Trade and Industry (DTI) refused to elaborate on reports of stalled talks on Wednesday, with a spokesman confining his comments to "A further constructive meeting was held."
The DTI also refused to comment on whether a new meeting date had been set for Beckett and van Miert to meet.
But despite the continued deadlock, analysts said the balance of probability for the deal being cleared had not changed.
One analyst said the latest news was "Pure brinkmanship as both sides take entrenched positions. I have no doubt it will end in compromise all round."
Chris Avery, airline analyst at Paribas said "I'm not changing my probability on whether the deal will be done."
"I still think it will go through. But we still have no real conclusion on the deal and no detailed timetable for conclusion. It may test the November deadline set by BA," he said.
BA chief executive Bob Ayling warned last month that if the deal did not receive clearance by November there was a danger it would have to be abandoned.
"There comes a point in any transaction where not having approval is tantamount to being told 'no'," he said.
Both BA and American were unavailable for an immediate comment earlier on Wednesday.

The deal faces a series of hurdles: clearance by the EU, clearance by Beckett on British competition grounds and by the U.S. authorities. But the deal is also conditional on an open skies pact to liberalise transatlantic traffic being sealed between the U.S. and Britain.
The last set of open skies talks ended without resolution earlier this year. The Department of Transport (DOT) told Reuters that no new date had been set for these talks.

"No new date has been set for open skies. Both governments are waiting for the DTI to clear the competition angle," said the DOT, which also declined to comment on the timetable for Beckett's final verdict.
Analysts said one development this week which could give BA and American some comfort was news that the U.S. had cleared the merger between U.S. aerospace giants Boeing Co and McDonnell Douglas Corp.
The deal was cleared by the U.S. Federal Trade Commission despite EU doubts. "Brussels will be chastened by the experience," said one analyst.

Paribas's Avery said there was always a danger that BA and American could find the final conditions for clearing the alliance too difficult to stomach. Such a scenario would scupper the mega-deal and be "a victory for small-mindedness" and demonstrate lack of understanding of the airline market.
